paras: The warning notices to Black residents of Bluffton, Indiana, were anonymous cards sent in late July and early August 1880 that told the town's few Black residents to leave and warned white residents to get rid of the Black people they employed or housed. No violence was reported, but Republican-leaning papers cited the warnings during the 1880 campaign as Democratic "Ku-Klux" intimidation.

A correspondent writing from Bluffton, the seat of Wells County, said the town had been without Black residents for twenty years, "the Democratic population always driving them out." By 1880 the only Black residents were the Waterman brothers, two barbers whom he called "quiet, peaceable citizens, and good Republicans."

In the days before August 5, several white residents received notices telling them to "part with the negroes they retain" and to "do it d—d quick." W. Waterman received a card signed "V. U. Q." telling him to get his "little band of negroes together and skip." Joseph Humphrey was told to get Black tenants out of his building, and the Central Hotel's proprietor, R. Rossington, and Sheriff J. B. Plessinger, a part owner, were warned about its Black cook. A Black man employed by the Watermans left town, saying he had been insulted every time he went on the street.
No report of arrests or of any action by the sheriff appears in the coverage.

The fullest account, a Bluffton dispatch of August 5 printed in the Chicago Daily Tribune on August 7, blamed "hot-headed Democrats" and said "work has really commenced on the Yazoo plan." On August 19 the Highland Weekly News of Hillsboro, Ohio, in a column urging a Garfield Club, reduced the story to three sentences: Bluffton appeared "infested with a gang of Ku-Klux" and its Black men had been notified to leave. That brief turned warnings addressed mostly to white employers and a landlord into notices served on Black men themselves.

A Cincinnati dispatch about a masked attack on Joshua Mack near Columbus, Indiana, printed by the Somerset Herald of Pennsylvania on August 25 under "Intimidation in Indiana," added only that "similar attempts at intimidation" had been made at Bluffton. None of the three printed a reply from Bluffton, and no coverage in the Black press was found.

reader.title: Warning notices to Black residents of Bluffton, Indiana
bases: Anonymous cards ordered the town's only Black residents to 'skip' and told white employers and a landlord to get rid of the Black people they employed or housed, in a town said to have driven out Black residents for twenty years; no forcible removal is reported (A1, A3).

Only the Aug. 5 Bluffton dispatch (A1) gives names, texts and detail; the Hillsboro brief (A3) and the one-line mention in a Cincinnati dispatch (A4) agree on Ku-Klux-style warnings at Bluffton but give no independent detail and may derive from the same reporting.

accounts.label: Bluffton correspondent
accounts.gist: Anonymous 'V. U. Q.' cards warned the Black barbers and the white people who employed or housed Black people; one Black man left; the writer blamed Democrats working 'the Yazoo plan' and expected a Ku-Klux march.

accounts.label: Ohio editorial brief
accounts.gist: Bluffton was 'infested with a gang of Ku-Klux' and its Black men had been notified to leave, as part of a Democratic 'Yazoo plan'.

accounts.label: Cincinnati dispatch
accounts.gist: After describing an attack near Columbus, Ind., it noted that 'similar attempts at intimidation' had been made at Bluffton and Shelbyville.

framing.detail: The Chicago Daily Tribune dispatch called Wells County 'notorious for its ultra Democratic capabilities and doings' and said 'work has really commenced on the Yazoo plan'.
The Highland Weekly News ran the item among campaign editorials urging a Garfield Club, blaming 'The Democracy' for 'the Yazoo plan'.
Under 'Intimidation in Indiana', the Somerset Herald's Cincinnati dispatch said Democratic threats of 'driving the negroes out of Indiana' were being carried out.

versions.value: Mostly white employers and a landlord told to get rid of Black workers and tenants, plus one card to the Black barber W. Waterman
'The colored men of that vicinity' notified to leave

conflicts.note: Not a true contradiction: the Hillsboro brief compresses the story. The dated Bluffton dispatch (A1) is the fuller and more direct source.
